stem: A project team needs to select a sub-group of 3 members from a pool of 8 candidates. In how many distinct ways can the sub-group be formed?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Selecting from 9 candidates instead of 8 gives C(9,3) = 84, an off-by-one error in the group size.
Dividing 8 x 7 x 6 = 336 by 2! instead of 3! gives 168; the full factorial of the selection size was not used.
Computing P(8,3) = 8 x 7 x 6 = 336 counts ordered arrangements, not unordered groups.

explanation: Because the sub-group has no internal ordering, use combinations: C(8,3) = 8! / (3! x 5!) = (8 x 7 x 6) / 6 = 56. Dividing by 3! (not 2! or 1!) removes all orderings of the chosen 3 members.

explanation_sections.punchline: A sub-group has no order, so use C(8,3) = 56. Using P(8,3) = 336 counts ordered arrangements, which the question does not ask for.
explanation_sections.approach: Ask: does the arrangement or sequence matter? If not, use combinations. Compute C(n,r) = (n * (n-1) * ... down r terms) / r!. Write the r! denominator before you multiply the numerator to avoid dividing by the wrong factorial.
explanation_sections.lesson: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered groups. The word 'select' or 'choose' without mention of rank or role signals combinations.
explanation_sections.timing: About 75 seconds. Numerator: 8 x 7 x 6 = 336. Denominator: 3! = 6. Divide: 56. Option (3) at 336 is the permutation answer; eliminate it in five seconds once you confirm order does not matter.
